Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Iowa statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Iowa property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • A property owner or aggrieved taxpayer may file a protest with the board of review on or after April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year. (Iowa Code 441.37; source)
  • Protest grounds: assessment not equitable compared with like property; assessed for more than authorized value; property not assessable, exempt or misclassified; error in assessment; fraud or misconduct (specifically stated). (Iowa Code 441.37; source)
  • Board of review decisions may be appealed to the Property Assessment Appeal Board within 20 days after the local board adjourns or May 31, whichever is later. (Iowa Code 441.37A; source)
  • The taxpayer may bypass PAAB and appeal the board of review decision directly to district court. (Iowa Code 441.37A; source)
  • District court appeal is filed with the clerk of district court within 20 days after the board's adjournment or May 31, whichever is later; the court hears it in equity with no presumption the assessment is correct. (Iowa Code 441.38; source)
  • Taxes on an assessment under appeal are not delayed; if reduced, taxes on the reduced portion are abated, refunded or credited. (Iowa Code 441.37A; source)
  • Property is valued at actual value and, except as otherwise provided, assessed at 100 percent of actual value. (Iowa Code 441.21; source)
  • The county treasurer offers delinquent parcels at public sale annually on the third Monday in June. (Iowa Code 446.7; source)
  • Redemption requires payment of the sale amount plus interest of two percent per month, each fraction counted as a full month. (Iowa Code 447.1; source)
Selling in Iowa?
We buy Iowa houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How to sell a Iowa house when this applies to you

  1. Find out what the title company needs. For an inherited or transferred house, that usually means the recorded deed or the probate paperwork that shows who owns it today.
  2. Get a payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  3. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs, not on the headline price.
  4. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. We buy houses as-is, with no repairs and no agent commission. See we buy houses in Iowa.

What a cash sale of a Iowa house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Iowa.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Iowa disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Iowa

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Iowa change, so confirm details with the official office or a Iowa attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Iowa

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

The closing agent pays unpaid tax from the sale proceeds at closing.

  • Claimants age 65 or older on or before January 1 of the assessment year qualify for an additional exemption of $6,500 of taxable value, applied in successive years without refiling. (Homestead Tax Credit and Exemption | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Claimants who received the homestead credit or exemption before July 1, 2026 are automatically awarded the 10% exemption without refiling if still eligible. (Homestead Tax Credit and Exemption | Department of Revenue; source)
  • The disabled veteran homestead tax credit is not eliminated by this change. (Homestead Tax Credit and Exemption | Department of Revenue; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Iowa statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

This guide covers Iowa foreclosure sales according to official sources. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • The officer must give four weeks' notice of the time and place of sale of real property. (Iowa Code 626.74; source)
  • Notice is posted in at least three public places in the county including the courthouse, plus two weekly newspaper publications for real estate, the first at least four weeks before sale. (Iowa Code 626.75; source)
  • Judgments for money or possession are enforced by execution. (Iowa Code 626.1; source)
  • After sale the debtor may redeem within one year and keeps possession meanwhile. (Iowa Code 628.3; source)
  • A defendant who stays in possession after foreclosure or execution sale is subject to forcible entry and detainer. (Iowa Code 648.1; source)
  • Iowa mortgages and deeds of trust may be foreclosed only by court action in equity, except under the alternative procedure of section 654.18. (Iowa Code 654.1; source)
  • Alternative nonjudicial voluntary foreclosure requires mutual written agreement; the mortgagor conveys all interest to the mortgagee and the mortgagee waives any deficiency. (Iowa Code 654.18; source)
  • Junior lienholders get 30 days from mailing of notice to exercise redemption rights under the voluntary procedure; mortgagor has a five-business-day cancellation right. (Iowa Code 654.18; source)
  • After a foreclosure sale the debtor may redeem within one year from the day of sale and keeps possession meanwhile; the first six months is exclusive to the debtor. (Iowa Code 628.3; source)
  • For mortgaged property under 10 acres, the mortgage may reduce the redemption period to six months (three months if not agricultural) if the mortgagee waives any deficiency. (Iowa Code 628.26; source)
  • Creditors may redeem within nine months from the day of sale if the debtor does not redeem. (Iowa Code 628.5; source)
  • For agricultural land, a creditor may not start foreclosure until it gives a notice of right to cure and waits 45 days. (Iowa Code 654.2A; source)

A Iowa deed is recorded with the county office named in the sources below. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • The statutory quitclaim form conveys 'all my interest' in the described real estate for stated consideration. (Iowa Code 558.19; source)
